How an Oregon property tax bill is built

Oregon bills each home on an assessed value that usually sits below its market value. The system comes from two ballot measures. Measure 5 (1990) keeps operating taxes at or below $15 per $1,000 of real market value, and voter-approved bonds fall outside that limit.

Measure 50 passed in May 1997 and changed how value is counted. As Clatsop County explains, first-year assessed value was set at the 1995 value minus 10 percent, and after that it can grow no more than 3 percent a year. Each taxing district also received a permanent rate that limits its operating tax authority.

Assessed value rises faster than 3 percent only in a short list of cases:

  • New improvements
  • Subdivisions and rezoning
  • Disqualification from a special assessment or exemption
  • Omitted property

Minor construction and ordinary maintenance are not added to assessed value. The tax year runs July 1 to June 30, and the assessment date is January 1.

Who sets and collects property tax?

The county assessor. Property taxes are set by and paid to the county assessor, and the Department of Revenue does not hold most residential and commercial property records.

The state agency handles centrally assessed companies and state-appraised industrial property. It also runs programs that matter to homeowners: the deferral program for disabled and senior homeowners, the forestland program, and the Property Value Appeals Board contacts. For questions about one house, call the county. The department's phone line is 503-378-4988, or 800-356-4222.

Each of Oregon's counties runs its own assessor office with its own website, payment options and forms, so use the office for the county where the house sits.

Due dates and penalties

The first installment is due November 15. The collector must mail or deliver statements by October 25 (ORS 311.250), and the schedule itself is in ORS 311.505.

Payment options, discounts and late charges
Payment optionDue date and discount or penalty
Pay everything by Nov. 153 percent discount

Multnomah County's payment FAQ adds details: if the 15th lands on a weekend or holiday, the due date moves to the next business day; payments are credited to the earliest tax year still owed; and a returned check carries a $25 fee and can cost the discount. Other counties may handle these points differently, so confirm with yours.

What happens to the tax bill when you sell

The tax follows the property, so any unpaid amount has to be settled at or before closing. Because the lien attaches on July 1 of the levy year, a sale in the middle of the fiscal year involves both taxes already billed and taxes that have not yet come due.

A yellow tax bill from Multnomah County means a mortgage company or a deferral program requested the information and may pay it. An owner who paid off a loan, changed lenders or cancelled a tax reserve should use that bill to pay directly. For how escrow handles the payoff at closing, ask the county assessment office or the mortgage company.

Missed installments carry the monthly interest shown above, so confirm the balance with the county before listing. A cash buyer will still expect the taxes to be current or paid from your proceeds at closing.

Senior and disability tax deferral

The deferral affects a sale. The state holds a lien for the deferred taxes plus interest, and a sale makes the balance due. The rules for the homestead deferral are in ORS chapter 311.

  • Applicants must be 62 or older by April 15 of the claim year, or have a disability, which means receiving or being eligible for federal Social Security disability or blindness benefits.
  • Combined household income for the prior year must be under $70,000, and net worth under $500,000, not counting the home.
  • The home must have been the claimant's homestead for at least five years, with exceptions.
  • Claims are filed between January 1 and April 15 before the tax year. Late claims run through December 1 with a fee.
  • Interest is 6 percent a year on taxes the state advanced.

Repayment comes due on the claimant's death, a sale or transfer of the property, loss of homestead status, or removal of a manufactured or floating home from Oregon. Payment is generally due by August 15 of the year after the event. Anyone who inherits the house may be jointly liable up to the property's equity, and the lien can be foreclosed like a purchase money mortgage.

A reverse mortgage generally blocks the program. Mortgage clauses that bar a homeowner from applying for deferral are void.

Foreclosure for unpaid property taxes

After three years, the county can foreclose. ORS 312.010 makes real property subject to foreclosure three years after the earliest delinquency date of the taxes levied.

The process gives the owner several chances to step in:

  • Notice goes by one newspaper publication and by delivery to owners of record, and the county must try to locate them.
  • The notice states the exact amount owed and describes the deferral programs.
  • The county holds the property two years from judgment. Eligible redeemers include prior owners, heirs, lienholders of record and municipalities.
  • Redeeming costs the full judgment amount, interest, a 5 percent penalty and a fee of $50, or the greater of $50 and the title search cost once the one-year notice has gone out.
  • At least a year before redemption ends, the tax collector must send certified and first-class mail with the amount owed, the end date, surplus rights and relief programs.

The former owner keeps possession during redemption, but waste on the property forfeits that right.

Who gets the money if the county sells a foreclosed home?

The former owner, or the owner's estate and heirs, if anything is left after the county's costs. ORS 312.520 to 312.560 lay out the steps.

If the house was the former owner's primary residence in a residential zone, the county must list it with an agent, and it needs an appraisal when its real market value is above $250,000. An auction follows if the property does not sell after three broker attempts or within 12 months. Auction rules include advertising for at least 30 days and a minimum bid of two-thirds of fair market value.

The surplus equals the property's value less allowable county costs, and the county must determine it within 60 days of the proceeds being deposited. Claims run through the State Treasurer, and heirs can claim without probate under listed conditions. Claimants have no interest in the surplus during the redemption period, and foreclosure does not erase the owner's other debts.

Redeeming before the period ends keeps the house out of a county sale, and the owner keeps whatever equity remains. Selling on your own terms before judgment usually leaves more in your pocket than waiting for the county.

Frequently asked questions

When are Oregon property taxes due?

November 15, February 15 and May 15, in three installments. Paying all of it by November 15 earns a 3 percent discount, and paying two-thirds earns 2 percent on that part. Interest on late amounts is 1 1/3 percent per month.

Who do I call about my Oregon property tax bill?

Your county assessor. Property taxes are set by and paid to the county, and the state Department of Revenue keeps few home records. The department can be reached at 503-378-4988 for state-level programs.

Can I defer my Oregon property taxes if I am retired?

Possibly. You must be 62 or older, or have a qualifying disability, and your household income must be under $70,000 with net worth under $500,000, among other tests. The state files a lien and charges 6 percent interest, and the balance comes due when you sell.

How long before Oregon can foreclose on unpaid property taxes?

Three years after the earliest delinquency date. After judgment, the county holds the property for two years, during which the owner or heirs can redeem it.

Does Oregon tax assessed value or market value?

Both appear in the system. Operating taxes are capped at $15 per $1,000 of real market value, and assessed value can grow only 3 percent a year in most cases.

What the Oregon homestead exemption protects

Oregon's homestead exemption shields part of the value of the home you live in from a creditor who holds a court judgment. It is a debt-collection rule found in ORS 18.395, and it is separate from any property tax break. You do not file anything to get it, because it applies by operation of law.

Two things matter to a seller. The exemption covers only a dollar slice of the equity, so a house worth far more than that slice can still be reached by a judgment creditor. And it follows the home through a sale only if the money is handled the right way afterward.

How much the exemption is now

For a single judgment debtor the exemption is $158,300 from July 1, 2026 until July 1, 2027, and $316,700 for two or more judgment debtors in the same household. The Oregon Judicial Department publishes an adjustment table, and the amounts now change each July 1.

PeriodOne judgment debtorTwo or more in a household
July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027$158,300$316,700
July 1, 2027 onwardSet by the State Court AdministratorSet by the State Court Administrator

Older printed copies of the statute and many websites still show $40,000 and $50,000. Those figures applied only before 2025, so check the court's adjustment table before relying on any number.

Who qualifies and what property counts

The home must be the actual residence of the owner, or of the owner's spouse, parent or child, and that person must occupy it. A temporary absence with the intent to return does not cost you the exemption.

  • The exemption reaches a purchaser's interest under a land sale contract.
  • It applies to manufactured dwellings and floating homes as defined in Oregon law.
  • ORS 18.402 limits the size of the homestead to 160 acres outside a platted town or city, or one block inside one.
  • It can apply to property located outside Oregon, based on an annotation citing a federal bankruptcy decision.

The full text of ORS 18.395 also covers what happens when the owner moves or sells. The exemption then continues for one year from the earliest of those events, which gives a household time to buy a replacement.

Which debts can still reach an Oregon homestead?

Four kinds of claims get past the exemption: construction liens, purchase money liens, lawfully executed mortgages, and a seller's enforcement of rights under a land sale contract. ORS 18.406 lists them.

Annotations to the statute add that a lien from a property division judgment in a divorce under ORS 107.105 is an exception as well. A mortgage lender, a contractor who improved the property and a spouse with a property division lien are therefore not held back by it.

Property tax is a different matter. A county can foreclose for delinquent taxes after three years from the earliest date of delinquency (ORS 312.010). A homeowner who is behind on taxes and also facing a judgment has two separate clocks running.

Selling a house that carries a judgment lien

A judgment against an owner can become a lien on real property in the county where the judgment is entered, but only if the court administrator notes in the register that it creates one. The lien reaches property the debtor owns when the judgment is entered and property acquired later, until the lien expires.

A seller who wants a clean closing can use the process in ORS 18.412. After signing an agreement to transfer a homestead, the owner or the buyer can send the judgment creditor a notice of intent to discharge the lien.

  • The notice goes by certified mail to the creditor.
  • It must describe the property and the judgment, state the fair market value and list each encumbrance.
  • It sets an objection date no earlier than 14 days after mailing.
  • If the property is worth more than senior liens plus the exemption, the excess, or the judgment amount if smaller, must be deposited with the court.
  • If the creditor does not object by the date, the property may be discharged from the lien without further notice.

If the creditor objects, the court decides the value or the other issues under ORS 18.415. Because the notice has to state the value and every encumbrance, consider having an attorney prepare it.

Sale proceeds under the homestead rule

The exemption can carry over to the money from a sale, but only if the proceeds are held for no more than one year and held with the intent to buy another homestead (ORS 18.395).

If you are selling to settle debts, keep the proceeds separate and documented. A clear record is the easiest way to show the money was set aside for a new home. A bankruptcy attorney can explain how a case changes the picture, and the statute fixes the home's value for these purposes at the earlier of the bankruptcy petition date or the transfer date.

Property tax deferral for seniors and disabled owners

This is a separate program from the creditor exemption. The state pays the county property taxes each November 15 for qualifying disabled and senior homeowners and places a lien on the home. It has to be repaid when the home is sold.

  • Household income limit: $70,000 for 2025 income.
  • Home value limit: real market value must fall within the county and years-of-residence limits, or under the $301,000 minimum cap.
  • Interest on deferred taxes: 6 percent simple interest per year.
  • Application deadline: April 15 with the county assessor.
  • Late application: April 16 to December 1, with a fee of 10 percent of taxes, between $20 and $180.
  • Recertification: every two years.

The lien is released about eight weeks after a payoff posts. A payoff received by October 30 can stop the state from paying that November's taxes if ownership changes after September 1. Details are on the Department of Revenue deferral page.

Veteran property tax exemption

Oregon offers a property tax exemption to an honorably discharged veteran with a 40 percent disability and to the unmarried surviving spouse of a veteran. The applicant or spouse must own the home and the applicant must live there.

In Deschutes County, applicants file with the assessor between January 1 and April 1 for the following tax year. An income limit applies only when a private physician, rather than the VA, documents the disability. Ask your own county assessor for the current exemption amount.

Frequently asked questions

How much is the Oregon homestead exemption in 2026?

$158,300 for one judgment debtor and $316,700 for two or more in the same household, for July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027. The Oregon Judicial Department lists the exact figures and the date each took effect.

Do I have to file a claim to get the Oregon homestead exemption?

No. The exemption is effective without a claim by the judgment debtor, so it applies automatically. Anyone facing a judgment sale or a lien discharge should ask an attorney how to raise it in that proceeding.

Does the homestead exemption protect my house from my mortgage lender?

No. ORS 18.406 says the exemption does not apply to lawfully executed mortgages, purchase money liens, construction liens or a seller's rights under a land sale contract.

How long can I hold the sale proceeds of my home and keep the exemption?

Up to one year, and only if you hold the money with the intent to buy another homestead. The year runs from the earliest of the move, absence or sale.

What is the Oregon property tax deferral income limit?

For 2026 the household income limit is $70,000, counting taxable and non-taxable income of the applicant and a spouse living in the home for calendar year 2025. The state charges 6 percent simple interest on the taxes it pays for you.

Does Oregon have an estate tax, and when does an estate owe it?

Yes. Oregon charges an estate transfer tax once the gross estate at death reaches $1 million and includes property Oregon can tax. A return is required at that level, and the tax applies to every resident decedent and to nonresidents who own Oregon real or tangible personal property (ORS 118.010).

The executor files, not the heirs. For a probated estate that is the court-appointed personal representative, and for a non-probate estate it is whoever holds the property. The return for deaths on or after January 1, 2012 is Form OR-706; the older Form IT-1 covered earlier deaths.

The $1 million line is not indexed for inflation. Real estate and retirement accounts both count toward it, which surprises families who assume only very large estates are covered.

Rates

Rates are graduated. They start at 10 percent on the part of the taxable estate over $1 million and climb to 16 percent above $9.5 million, with smaller steps in between at each higher bracket. For each bracket, the tax is a base amount plus the bracket's rate on the excess over its lower limit. The Department of Revenue's Form OR-706 instructions carry the full bracket table, and the personal representative or an estate attorney applies it to the taxable estate. Because the top rate only applies to the slice above the last bracket line, most estates that owe tax pay an overall rate well below the headline figures, and the real number depends on deductions, the marital election and any out-of-state property.

How the Oregon taxable estate is calculated

The calculation begins with the federal taxable estate and is adjusted by statute. State death taxes deductible under federal law are added back, and the value of Oregon special marital property and qualifying natural resource property is subtracted, among other items.

  • Bequests to a surviving spouse can be deducted, and a marital or QTIP claim needs an Oregon-only Schedule M.
  • An executor may make an Oregon special marital property election on the return, and elections made for state purposes are irrevocable.
  • The second spouse's estate must include property previously claimed for a QTIP or special marital deduction.

For a resident with property in other states, the table amount is multiplied by a ratio. The numerator is Oregon real and tangible property plus intangibles, and the denominator is the gross estate. For a nonresident, only Oregon real and tangible property goes in the numerator, which is why an out-of-state owner of an Oregon rental or cabin can face an Oregon filing.

Due dates and penalties

For deaths on or after January 1, 2022, the return and payment are due 12 months after the date of death. Earlier deaths had a nine-month deadline, so confirm the date of death first.

Filing itemRule
Return requiredGross estate of $1 million or more
Due date, death on or after 1/1/202212 months after death
Extension to fileSix months, using Form OR-706 EXT
Extension to payOnly in special circumstances, under OAR 150-118-0150
Fiduciary income returnForm OR-41 if a probated estate had any gross income

An extension to file does not extend the time to pay, and interest runs on unpaid tax. A 5 percent penalty applies for late filing or payment, rising to 25 percent in total when the return is more than three months late. Payment goes to the Department of Revenue, which gives a receipt to whoever pays (ORS 118.250).

If you are late on a return or unsure about a date of death, call the Estate/Fiduciary Tax Unit at 503-378-4988 right away.

How estate tax affects selling the inherited house

The house is part of the gross estate at its date-of-death value, and that same value generally becomes the heir's basis. IRS Publication 551 sets inherited property basis at fair market value on the date of death, or the alternate valuation date if the personal representative elected it.

That helps a seller. If the home sells soon after the death at about the appraised value, there is often little or no income gain to report, even if the owner bought it decades ago.

The estate may still face a cash problem. A house can be the largest asset in a taxable estate while the tax is due in cash. Installment payment of the tax is possible, with a first mortgage on Oregon real property as possible collateral. If the extension to pay runs more than 12 months, the estate must provide collateral equal to twice the unpaid tax.

Does nonresident withholding apply to a sale by the estate?

Not for a court-supervised sale. Sales by an estate's personal representative or executor, a conservator or a bankruptcy trustee are exempt from escrow withholding.

Other exemptions are narrower:

  • The price, including assumed debt, is $100,000 or less.
  • The tax to be withheld would be under $100 per transferor.
  • The transfer happens through foreclosure or a sheriff's sale.

Outside those cases the escrow agent may ask the seller for Form OR-18-WC. A nonresident heir who has Oregon-source income from the sale also files Form OR-40-N. Keep the form with the estate records rather than sending it to the department.

What an executor should gather before listing an Oregon house

Collect the date of death, a value for every asset and the paperwork that shows who is acting for the estate. A return is needed at $1 million, so the total of all assets drives every other step.

  • A date-of-death valuation of the house, which also supports the heirs' basis.
  • Statements for retirement accounts, bank accounts and any out-of-state property.
  • Proof of who the personal representative is, since that person files Form OR-706.
  • Any prior spouse's estate return that used a marital or QTIP election.

The Estate/Fiduciary Tax Unit is at PO Box 14110, Salem, OR 97309-0910. Phone lines run 7:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday through Friday, except 9 to 11 a.m. on Thursdays and holidays.

Checking which law applies to your date of death

Estate tax thresholds and deadlines have changed before, and the rules that apply are the ones in force on the date of death. Ask the department or an attorney which version covers your estate, especially when the death date sits near a change in the law.

For help with an inherited house in Oregon, contact the department's estate team at estate.help.dor@dor.oregon.gov, or the general line at 800-356-4222. This is general information, not legal or tax advice.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Oregon estate tax exemption?

The filing threshold is a gross estate of $1 million or more. Rates start at 10 percent on the taxable estate over $1 million and reach 16 percent above $9.5 million.

Is there an Oregon inheritance tax that heirs pay?

The tax is imposed on the estate, and the executor files Form OR-706. The earlier Form IT-1 was used for deaths before January 1, 2012.

How long does an estate have to file the Oregon return?

For deaths on or after January 1, 2022, the return and payment are due 12 months after death. A six-month extension to file is available, but it does not extend the time to pay.

Does a nonresident who inherits Oregon real estate owe Oregon estate tax?

The estate can owe tax when a nonresident decedent owned Oregon real or tangible personal property and the gross estate reaches $1 million. Only the Oregon property is counted in the ratio.

Can I sell an inherited Oregon house before the estate tax is paid?

Call the Estate/Fiduciary Tax Unit at 503-378-4988 to find out what applies to your estate before you set a closing date.

How an eviction case works in Oregon

An Oregon eviction is a court case that decides one thing: who gets possession of the home. It is an action by a landlord to remove a tenant from a rented dwelling, and it covers houses, apartments, mobile homes and floating homes alike. Back rent and damage claims are not decided in that case.

A landlord has to use the court. Private eviction help is not permitted, and removing a tenant without a court order is illegal. For an owner thinking about a sale, that rule sets the pace for everything that follows.

  • The landlord serves a written notice and waits for the notice period to end.
  • The landlord files a complaint and summons with a copy of the notice.
  • A first appearance is set, and the tenant answers or settles.
  • If the case is contested, the court holds a trial.
  • After a judgment for possession, the landlord asks for a notice of restitution and, if needed, a writ of execution carried out by the sheriff.

Typical deadlines from filing to move-out

Most Oregon eviction cases reach a first appearance within about one to two weeks of filing, and a contested trial follows within about another two to four weeks. Local practice differs slightly between counties.

StepTiming
First appearance, most casesAbout one week after filing
First appearance, nonpaymentAbout two weeks after filing
First appearance, Multnomah CountyTypically 7 to 14 days out, or 15 to 21 days for certain nonpayment cases
First appearance, Coos County7 to 15 days after filing
Written answerSame day as the first appearance (ORS 105.137)
Trial, nonpayment claims15 to 30 days after the appearance
Trial, other claimsNo later than 15 days after the appearance
Judgment valid for restitution60 days
Writ must be servedWithin 30 days of issuance

The text of ORS 105.137 protects the tenant when a trial slips past those windows. If the delay is not the landlord's doing, the court can order the tenant to pay accruing rent into court after a hearing finds that order fair.

What happens at the first appearance?

The first appearance ends in a default judgment, a dismissal, a settlement, or a trial date. If the landlord shows up and the tenant does not, the court can enter a judgment of restitution for the landlord. If the tenant shows up and the landlord does not, the tenant can get a dismissal and costs.

An unrepresented tenant who wants to fight must file a written answer on the court form and serve the landlord the same day (ORS 105.137). In Coos County the answer is due by 4:00 p.m. that day, along with a fee or a request to defer it. The form lists defenses such as missing repairs, retaliation, a defective notice, and status as a victim of domestic violence or stalking.

Settlement is possible at any point, and the parties can ask a judge to approve the agreement. If the tenant then breaks it, the landlord can file a declaration of non-compliance and ask for a judgment of restitution.

How an eviction notice must be delivered

A written notice under the landlord-tenant chapter can be handed over, sent by first class mail, or, only if the written rental agreement allows it, mailed and attached to the door. Email counts only when the parties signed a separate written addendum after the tenant moved in.

Mailing adds time. Under ORS 90.155, a notice sent by first class mail has its compliance or termination period extended by three days, and the notice has to say so. The notice must also give the right number of days, because a defective notice is one of the defenses on the tenant's answer form. A termination notice sent by email must also go by first class mail.

Write down the delivery date and method before anything is filed. Those records also tell a buyer exactly where the case stands.

When a landlord can use a 24-hour notice

A 24-hour written notice is allowed only for the serious acts listed in ORS 90.396, and the notice must name the act and the date and time the tenancy ends. The statute covers a tenant, someone under the tenant's control, or in some cases the tenant's pet.

  • Seriously threatening or inflicting substantial injury on someone who is not a tenant.
  • Recklessly creating a serious risk of substantial injury to a non-tenant on the premises.
  • Inflicting substantial injury on a neighbor nearby.
  • Intentionally causing substantial damage to the premises.
  • Giving substantially false information about a criminal conviction on the rental application, if the landlord ends the tenancy within 30 days of finding out.
  • Committing an act described as outrageous in the extreme, such as unlawful drug manufacture or distribution, burglary or a bias crime.

A Court of Appeals decision requires the actual date and time to appear in the notice (see the statute text). Pet-related notices must describe the tenant's right to cure by removing the pet.

What a landlord may not do during an eviction

A landlord may not change the locks, remove the tenant, or shut off essential services, and may not seriously threaten to do any of those things. ORS 90.375 lists lockouts and the willful loss of heat, water, hot water or electricity.

The remedy is costly for the owner. The tenant can seek an order to return to the home, and can end the rental agreement and recover up to two months of periodic rent or twice the actual damages, whichever is greater. The tenant does not have to get an injunction or move back in first. Anyone tempted to speed up a vacancy before a sale should read that section carefully.

Belongings left in the house

After a tenancy ends, the landlord must give written notice before storing or selling anything the tenant left, and then wait out a response period. ORS 90.425 sets five days after hand delivery or eight days after mailing for ordinary personal property, and 45 days for a manufactured dwelling or floating home.

A landlord may also dispose of low-value items without a sale. The thresholds are $1,000 for ordinary property, $4,000 for a recreational vehicle and $8,000 for a manufactured dwelling or floating home. The rule applies when a tenant has been gone seven days after a court eviction order that was not carried out, and when the landlord has regained possession from the sheriff after a writ.

A landlord who follows the steps in good faith has a full defense to claims for the lost items. One who does not can owe up to twice the tenant's actual damages. Any sale that depends on an empty house has to wait for that notice period to run.

Eviction and selling a rented house

An open eviction case and the tenant's rights stay tied to the house, so any buyer will care about possession and notice defects. The court will not rule on back rent in the same case.

  • Eviction court decides possession only. A claim for unpaid rent or damage goes to small claims if it is $10,000 or less.
  • A judgment of restitution is good for 60 days, so a sale timeline built around move-out should account for it.
  • The sheriff, not the landlord, carries out the writ.
  • A defective notice is a listed defense, so check the notice before a case is filed.

Owners with a tenant in place, a case in progress, or a house full of old belongings sometimes choose a buyer who will take the property as it stands, with the tenant situation unresolved. That avoids months of court steps before a sale. Contact us if you want to talk through the house and the lease.

Frequently asked questions

How long does an eviction take in Oregon?

A contested case often runs several weeks from filing to trial. The first appearance usually comes about one to two weeks after filing, and ORS 105.137 puts a trial for nonpayment 15 to 30 days after that appearance. Notice periods before filing, plus the time for a notice of restitution and a writ, add more time.

Can I evict a tenant myself in Oregon without going to court?

No. Changing locks, removing a tenant or cutting off utilities is prohibited by ORS 90.375, and a tenant can recover up to two months of rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater. A landlord has to win a judgment and use the court process.

What if the tenant does not show up to the first appearance?

The court may enter a default judgment of restitution for the landlord. Missing the date can mean an automatic loss and an eviction on the tenant's record, though a tenant with a good reason can ask to set the judgment aside.

How long does a landlord have to store a tenant's belongings?

The tenant gets a written notice and then a response period of at least five days after hand delivery or eight days after mailing for ordinary property. Items worth $1,000 or less, or so little that storage and sale would cost more than a sale brings, may be disposed of under ORS 90.425.

Can I sell a house while an eviction is pending in Oregon?

The case and the tenant's rights stay with the property. A buyer will want the notice, proof of service and court file, and your timeline should account for the 60 days a judgment stays good for restitution. Check with a lawyer or title company on your facts.

What a quitclaim deed transfers in Oregon

It transfers whatever interest the grantor has on the date of the deed, and nothing more. ORS 93.865 gives a short statutory form in which the grantor "releases and quitclaims" all right, title and interest in the described property.

Legal and equitable interests both pass, title the grantor acquires later does not pass, and the deed does not work as an estoppel. A grantee does not lose good faith purchaser status just because the title came by quitclaim.

Oregon has two other statutory deed forms, and comparing them shows where a quitclaim fits.

Oregon's three statutory deed forms
DeedWhat the grantor promises
Warranty deed (ORS 93.850)Grantor is seized of the estate, the property is free of encumbrances except as stated, and the grantor will defend title against lawful claims. After-acquired title passes.
Special warranty deed (ORS 93.855)Same effect, but the encumbrance promise covers only what the grantor created or allowed, and the warranty covers claims by, through or under the grantor.
Quitclaim deed (ORS 93.865)No covenants. Conveys the grantor's interest on the deed date, whatever it is.

When a quitclaim deed makes sense

It works best between people who already know the title history, such as spouses, parents and children, or co-owners sorting out who holds what. The grantor makes no covenants, so the grantee relies on the grantor's actual interest and nothing else.

Common uses include:

  • Adding or removing a spouse or family member from a deed
  • Moving a house into or out of a family trust
  • Clearing a possible claim from someone who may have had an interest
  • Splitting up co-owned property after a separation

A federal statute helps with some of these transfers. Under 12 U.S.C. 1701j-3(d), a lender may not enforce a due-on-sale clause on a home of fewer than five units for transfers such as one to a spouse or children, one to a relative after the borrower dies, one under a divorce decree, or one into a living trust where the borrower stays a beneficiary and keeps occupancy. That law covers the lender's clause only, so read the other loan terms separately.

What the deed must include before the county records it

Four items come up most often, and one of them can block recording. The consideration statement in ORS 93.030 has to appear on the face of an instrument that conveys fee title, and a county recording officer may not accept the instrument for recording without it.

  • Consideration. The true and actual consideration paid, written on the deed (ORS 93.030).
  • Mandatory notice. The all-caps statement in ORS 93.040(1) telling the person transferring title to inquire about their rights, and stating that the instrument does not allow use of the property in violation of land use laws. An omission leads to an action only if the buyer would not have accepted the deed without it.
  • Tax statement address. The line beginning "Until a change is requested, all tax statements shall be sent to the following address" (ORS 93.260). Leaving it out does not invalidate the conveyance.
  • Legal description. ORS 93.600 allows a subdivision, lot and block, plat parcel, metes and bounds, or a book and page reference. A tax lot number alone is not adequate.

Deeds also have to be signed by the grantors and acknowledged before a judge, justice of the peace or notary within the state (ORS 93.410). No seal is required. Any restriction that bars use or sale based on race, religion or similar characteristics is void under ORS 93.270.

Recording rules and fees

The county clerk records deeds and mortgages affecting real property under ORS 205.130, and the fees are set in statute. The base fee under ORS 205.320 is $5 for each page, with a $5 minimum, and a page is one side of a sheet no larger than 14 by 8.5 inches.

Three more charges come on top of that under ORS 205.323: $1 for the Oregon Land Information System, $10 split among the county, the clerk and the assessment and taxation fund, and $60 to the assessment and taxation fund. Some filings, such as satisfactions of judgment, are exempt.

Format rules also apply: 10-point type or larger (ORS 205.232), and paper no larger than 14 inches by 8 1/2 inches. The first page needs the transaction names, party names and a delivery contact, plus the consideration and tax statement information for fee conveyances (ORS 205.234). If first-page items are missing, a cover sheet can be attached and recorded with the instrument. The clerk notes the day, hour and minute of recording (ORS 205.180) and then returns the instrument to the person who recorded it or is authorized to receive it.

Why recording order matters

An unrecorded deed can lose to a later buyer. ORS 93.640 makes an unrecorded conveyance void against a later good faith purchaser for value whose instrument is recorded first.

If a family keeps a signed quitclaim in a drawer, a second deed from the same grantor can end up ahead of it in line. ORS 93.620 treats an instrument as recorded at the time the clerk certifies, and the county clerk keeps indexes listing the names of all parties (ORS 93.630).

A memorandum can be recorded in place of the full instrument. It must state the date, the parties, a legal description and the nature of the interest, and be signed and acknowledged. A memorandum of a fee conveyance must also state the consideration.

Is there a transfer tax on a deed?

Oregon bars new real estate transfer taxes. Voters approved Measure 79 on November 6, 2012, by 58.89 percent to 41.11 percent. The amendment prohibits the state and local governments from taxing, charging or assessing the transfer of an interest in real property, or measuring a charge by the price paid.

It exempted any tax, fee or assessment already in effect and operative on December 31, 2009. Still budget for recording charges, any title or escrow charges, and the county fees above. Those apply to a family quitclaim the same way they apply to any other deed.

Co-owners named on one deed

A deed to two or more people creates a tenancy in common unless it clearly says the owners have a right of survivorship. A deed to spouses married to each other creates a tenancy by the entirety unless it says otherwise. Under ORS 93.180 and 93.190, joint tenancy is abolished except for conveyances to trustees or personal representatives.

This matters for quitclaims between family members. A quitclaim to a spouse and a child without careful wording leaves a tenancy in common, and each owner's share can pass to that owner's own heirs. When the house is later sold, each co-owner's interest has to be conveyed.

A quitclaim also cannot change how title passes at death. Under ORS 114.215, a decedent's title vests in the heirs or devisees, subject to administration and sale by the personal representative. A deed signed by one heir before probate conveys only that heir's interest.

Mistakes that make a quitclaim useless for a sale

Most failures come from skipping a statutory step or expecting the deed to do more than the statute says.

  • Leaving out the consideration statement, which keeps the clerk from recording it
  • Describing the house by tax lot number alone
  • Using paper or type that does not meet the recording size rules
  • Forgetting to record, so a later recorded deed wins
  • Assuming a quitclaim fixes defects or liens that existed before it, when it passes only the grantor's interest
  • Signing for an estate asset without court authority

A quitclaim can help in a cash sale when the seller needs to clean up a name on the title before closing. It cannot hand over title the grantor does not hold. If the title has gaps, ask the title company what it needs before the closing date is set.

Frequently asked questions

Does an Oregon quitclaim deed need to be notarized?

Yes. ORS 93.410 requires deeds to be signed by the grantors and acknowledged before a judge, justice of the peace or notary public in the state. A seal is not required.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Oregon?

The base fee is $5 per page with a $5 minimum, plus $1, $10 and $60 added by ORS 205.323. A county clerk's office can confirm the current total for your page count.

Is there an Oregon transfer tax on a quitclaim deed?

Oregon does not allow new transfer taxes after Measure 79 passed in 2012, except for any that were already operating on December 31, 2009. Recording and other filing fees still apply.

Can a quitclaim deed remove someone from a mortgage?

A quitclaim deed changes who holds title, because ORS 93.865 passes the grantor's interest. Whether anyone is released from the loan is a matter for the lender, so ask before you sign. Federal law on due-on-sale clauses, 12 U.S.C. 1701j-3(d), limits lender enforcement for certain family transfers.

What is the difference between a quitclaim and a warranty deed in Oregon?

A warranty deed under ORS 93.850 carries promises about ownership, encumbrances and defending title, and passes later-acquired title. A quitclaim under ORS 93.865 carries none of those promises and passes only the grantor's interest on the date of the deed.

The law behind Oregon's transfer on death deed

Oregon's transfer on death deed comes from the Uniform Real Property Transfer on Death Act, found at ORS 93.948 to 93.979. The legislature passed it as chapter 212 of the 2011 Oregon Laws, effective January 1, 2012.

What matters is the date of death: any owner who dies on or after January 1, 2012 is covered, whenever the deed was signed. Wills, trusts and joint ownership remain open as other routes, and nothing in the act displaces them.

ORS 93.949 defines the terms. The transferor is the living person who signs, the property is any real estate interest in Oregon, and the beneficiary is whoever receives it through the deed. A deed can name primary beneficiaries and alternates, who take only if no primary beneficiary survives or qualifies (ORS 93.953).

Transfer on death deed rules at a glance

Oregon transfer on death deed rules by question
QuestionAnswer (statute)
When does the beneficiary get the property?At the owner's death, not before (ORS 93.953, 93.967)
Must it be recorded?Yes, before the owner dies, in the deed records of the county where the property sits (ORS 93.961)
Does the beneficiary need to accept it or give anything?No notice, delivery, acceptance or consideration is required (ORS 93.963)
Can the owner change their mind?Yes, even if the deed says otherwise (ORS 93.955)
Time to contest capacity, fraud or undue influence18 months after the owner's death (ORS 93.959)
Time for estate to reach the property for creditor claims18 months after the owner's death (ORS 93.973)
Effect of divorce after recordingGifts to the former spouse are revoked unless the deed shows a different intent (ORS 93.981)

What the deed must contain

Start with everything a recordable lifetime deed requires. Then add wording that the transfer takes effect at the owner's death, and name the person who will receive the house. ORS 93.961 voids a designation that names beneficiaries only as members of a class.

ORS 93.975 offers an optional fill-in form. A deed written on it contains:

  • The names and mailing addresses of the owners signing.
  • A legal description of the property.
  • A primary beneficiary and an alternate beneficiary.
  • The address where the county clerk should send tax statements.
  • A return address for the recorded deed.
  • A statement that the owner can revoke it, and a warning that it must be recorded before death to be effective.
  • Signatures and a notary acknowledgment block.

The form itself suggests reading it closely and thinking about a lawyer. Errors such as a wrong legal description or a missing signature tend to surface only after the owner has died, when nothing can be corrected.

Recording costs

The fee depends on the county. In Multnomah County, recording a deed costs $86 for the first page and $5 for each additional page.

Some deeds draw added charges there. If the document has no blank space for the county's 4 inch by 2 inch recording label, a cover page is needed, at $5. A cover page that fails the statutory first-page requirements adds a $20 non-standard fee. Every extra transaction in a single document costs $5, as does each extra reference to an assignment, release or satisfaction.

Other Oregon counties set their own schedules. Phone the clerk or recorder in the house's county before mailing anything, since a rejected deed does no one any good.

What the owner can still do after signing

While the owner is living, nothing changes in who is in charge. Under ORS 93.967 the deed does not affect the owner's rights, including the right to transfer or encumber the property, and it gives the beneficiary no present interest, even if the beneficiary knows about it.

That means the house can still be sold, refinanced or pledged for a loan. The deed also does not change the rights of the owner's creditors, and it does not change whether the owner or the beneficiary qualifies for public or medical assistance as defined in ORS 414.025. The beneficiary's creditors cannot reach the property either, because the beneficiary has no legal or equitable interest during the owner's life.

An owner who wants out has three recorded options under ORS 93.965:

  • A new transfer on death deed that revokes the earlier one, expressly or through inconsistent terms.
  • A recorded instrument that expressly revokes it, in whole or in part.
  • A lifetime deed that transfers the same interest, to the extent of that transfer.

Whichever route is used, it has to be acknowledged and recorded in the county deed records while the owner is alive. An agent can revoke only when the deed expressly grants that power. Tearing up or writing on a recorded deed does not work, because a recorded deed cannot be revoked by an act on the deed itself.

What happens to the house when the owner dies?

Whoever is named as beneficiary receives the house together with whatever is attached to it: liens, mortgages and other encumbrances. Under ORS 93.969 the beneficiary takes subject to all conveyances and encumbrances, and that includes state claims for public or medical assistance reimbursement when the probate estate cannot cover them.

That section also sets out these rules:

  • A beneficiary who dies before the owner gets nothing, and that share does not pass under the deed.
  • When there are several beneficiaries, each gets an equal undivided share with no survivorship, and a lapsed share is divided among the rest in proportion.
  • If the owner held title as a joint tenant, the surviving joint owner takes first, and the deed operates only after the last joint owner dies.
  • No covenant or warranty of title comes with the transfer, even when the deed claims one.

A beneficiary can also give up the inheritance. ORS 93.971 lets a beneficiary disclaim all or part of the interest, with the procedure in ORS 105.623 through 105.649.

Challenges and creditor claims

Both can happen, but a challenge has an 18 month limit that starts at the owner's death. The mental capacity needed to sign or revoke the deed is the same as for a will, and any deed or revocation produced by fraud, duress or undue influence is void (ORS 93.959). A person who wants to raise those issues has to file within that window.

For debts, ORS 93.973 allows the estate to go after the transferred house only when the probate estate falls short. It covers claims allowed or established against the estate under ORS 114.505 to 114.560 or ORS chapter 115, and statutory allowances owed to a surviving spouse or child under ORS 114.015. If the owner signed several deeds, liability is split among those properties in proportion to each one's net value at death.

A divorce changes things as well. If the marriage ends by divorce or annulment after the deed is recorded, ORS 93.981 cancels any gift to the former spouse, as though that person had died first, unless the deed states a different wish.

Selling an Oregon house with a transfer on death deed

A living owner can sell the house as freely as any other. The beneficiary gets no vote, and once the house is sold the deed has nothing left to transfer.

After the owner's death, the beneficiary receives the house with no probate transfer. The two 18 month windows in ORS 93.959 and ORS 93.973 are the dates to raise with a title company or attorney before closing a sale. A beneficiary who inherits a house with a mortgage, repair needs or tax bills takes it as-is with those attached.

Plenty of beneficiaries live far away and would rather not run a rental or maintain an empty home. We buy Oregon houses as-is for cash, and you can ask us for an offer once you have the recorded deed and the death certificate in hand. A local attorney or the title company should confirm the steps for your county. Gather the deed, the death certificate, a mortgage payoff figure and recent tax bills ahead of time so a closing is not held up.

Frequently asked questions

Does a transfer on death deed avoid probate in Oregon?

It can, since the house passes at death under the deed itself. Creditors of the estate may still reach it if the probate estate cannot cover their claims, for up to 18 months after death (ORS 93.973).

Does the beneficiary have to sign or accept an Oregon TOD deed?

No. ORS 93.963 says the deed does not need notice to, delivery to, or acceptance by the beneficiary during the owner's life, and it needs no consideration.

Can I sell my house after recording a transfer on death deed?

Yes. Under ORS 93.967 the deed does not limit your right to sell or borrow against the property while you are alive, and the beneficiary has no present interest.

How do I cancel an Oregon transfer on death deed?

Record a new deed, a revocation instrument, or a lifetime deed of the same interest, each acknowledged and recorded in the county deed records before you die (ORS 93.965). Marking up the recorded deed does not revoke it.

Where do I record a transfer on death deed in Oregon?

In the deed records of the county clerk's office for the county where the property is located (ORS 93.961). In Multnomah County the fee is $86 for the first page and $5 for each added page.

Does Oregon tax the profit when you sell a house?

Oregon applies one rate table to taxable income, with no separate rate for long-term gains. Residents pay under the table below, and the lower brackets are adjusted each year for inflation.

Taxable income (base schedule)Oregon tax
Up to $2,0004.75 percent
$2,000 to $5,000$95 plus 6.75 percent of the excess over $2,000
$5,000 to $125,000$298 plus 8.75 percent of the excess over $5,000
Over $125,000$10,798 plus 9.9 percent of the excess over $125,000

The top bracket is not indexed. A large gain can push part of a year's income into the 9.9 percent bracket, so the size of your other income in the sale year matters.

The federal home sale exclusion

Gain on your main home is excludable up to $250,000, or $500,000 for a joint return. Ownership counts first: you or your spouse need 24 months of ownership inside the five years ahead of the sale. For the larger amount, each spouse also needs 24 months of living there as a main home in that same window.

A second exclusion is generally off the table if you took one on a different home sold during the previous two years. A Form 1099-S from the closing means the sale gets reported even if every dollar of gain is excludable; any taxable portion belongs on Schedule D and Form 8949.

  • Lived in and owned it for 24 of the last 60 months: probably eligible.
  • Rented it out most of the last five years: the use test may fail.
  • Took an exclusion on another sale in the past two years: the limit may apply.

We do not give tax advice. Have a preparer check your actual dates, particularly if you moved out before listing.

Gain above the exclusion

Whatever exceeds the exclusion is a federal capital gain and Oregon taxable income. Owning the house longer than a year makes the gain long-term, which carries federal rates of 0, 15 and 20 percent. The 0 percent rate started at $48,350 for single filers and $96,700 for joint filers in 2025. Those cutoffs shift annually, so look up the current ones while you plan.

Two other items matter for real estate:

  • Unrecaptured section 1250 gain on real property tops out at a 25 percent rate. Ask a preparer whether earlier rental depreciation created some.
  • The net investment income tax (IRS Topic 559) may apply to higher earners.

A house held one year or less produces short-term gain, taxed as ordinary income. Oregon residents then owe state tax on top.

How to work out your gain

Your gain equals what you realize from the sale less adjusted basis. Basis begins with the purchase price and buying costs. Improvements that add value raise it; depreciation and casualty insurance payouts lower it.

Inherited houses follow another rule. IRS Publication 551 sets basis at fair market value on the date of death, or on the alternate valuation date when the personal representative chose that election. A house inherited and sold soon after often shows little gain for that reason.

Dig out your purchase closing statement and receipts for big projects like a new roof or kitchen remodel. A preparer needs both ends of the equation, not only the sale price. Depreciation claimed while the house was a rental lowers basis and can raise the taxable gain.

Selling Oregon real estate from out of state

Oregon taxes nonresidents on income from Oregon sources, and gain from selling Oregon real property counts (ORS 316.127). Full-year nonresidents use the same rate table on that Oregon-source income, and the nonresident return is Form OR-40-N.

The escrow agent may have to withhold Oregon tax at closing. The amount is the least of four percent of the consideration, the net proceeds, or eight percent of the gain includible in Oregon taxable income. The transferor completes the seller sections of Form OR-18-WC, signs it and gives it to the escrow agent, who completes the rest. Keep the form with your tax records; it does not go to the Department of Revenue.

A sale is exempt from withholding when:

  • The consideration, including assumed debt, is $100,000 or less.
  • The home is your personal residence and no federal income tax is owed on the sale.
  • A credit for tax paid to the home state means no Oregon tax is likely.
  • The tax to be withheld is under $100 per transferor.
  • The transfer avoids foreclosure with no additional payment, or occurs through foreclosure or a sheriff's sale.
  • A court-supervised sale occurs, such as one by a personal representative or bankruptcy trustee.

Withholding is not the final tax. A nonresident still files Form OR-40-N when Oregon gross income exceeds the filing threshold, even if the sale was exempt, and the withheld amount is credited on that return. Oregon residents are exempt transferors.

When payment is due on the tax from a sale

For a resident, the tax is settled on the annual Oregon return. Estimated payments are generally needed if you expect to owe $1,000 or more after credits and withholding. A large gain in a single year can meet that test, so some sellers make an estimated payment in the year of the sale.

A simple plan:

  1. Gather the purchase documents, improvement receipts and the closing statement.
  2. Estimate gain and subtract any exclusion you qualify for.
  3. Compare expected tax with withholding and credits for the year.
  4. Decide whether an estimated payment is needed before the next quarter's date.

The Department of Revenue can be reached at 503-378-4988 or 800-356-4222 or by email at questions.dor@dor.oregon.gov. Estimated tax rules for nonresidents are narrower: they apply only to income subject to Oregon withholding, from an Oregon business or lottery winnings over $600. A nonresident should read the instructions on the department's website.

How a cash sale changes the tax picture

Selling for cash does not rewrite the tax rules. You figure gain from the same price, basis and exclusion, and a title or escrow company still handles the closing, so any withholding step described earlier still takes place there.

Questions that come up for owners considering a fast as-is sale:

  • Will I owe Oregon tax? It depends on your gain, exclusion and residency.
  • Must I report a sale whose gain is fully excluded? Yes, when a Form 1099-S arrives.
  • Does living out of state trigger withholding? It can, unless an exemption fits.

Treat this page as general information. Run your own numbers past a tax professional or the Department of Revenue.

Frequently asked questions

Does Oregon have a capital gains tax on home sales?

Oregon taxes gain on a home sale as part of income, with rates from 4.75 percent to 9.9 percent under ORS 316.037. The federal exclusion of $250,000 or $500,000 can remove all or part of the gain first.

What is the Oregon withholding on a nonresident home sale?

The escrow agent withholds the least of four percent of the consideration, the net proceeds, or eight percent of the gain includible in Oregon income, unless an exemption applies. Form OR-18-WC documents the calculation.

Do I report a home sale if the gain is under the exclusion?

Yes, if you received Form 1099-S, the sale must be reported even when all gain is excludable. Report any taxable part on Schedule D and Form 8949.

Is gain on an inherited house taxed in Oregon?

Only gain over the stepped-up basis is taxed, since basis is generally the fair market value at the date of death. A sale soon after inheriting often shows little gain.

Who do I call with questions about Oregon tax on a sale?

Call the Oregon Department of Revenue at 503-378-4988 or 800-356-4222, or email questions.dor@dor.oregon.gov.

Sheriff sale versus trustee's sale

A sheriff sells the house after a court judgment, while a trustee sells it under a trust deed without a court case. Oregon uses both, and the rules for notice, timing and what follows the sale differ.

The three ways an Oregon house can be sold at a foreclosure or judgment sale
Sale typeWho runs itTiming and rules
Trustee's sale (nonjudicial)The trustee named in the trust deedHeld after 9 a.m. and before 4 p.m. in a county where the property sits (ORS 86.782). Notice is served or mailed at least 120 days ahead (ORS 86.764).
Judicial foreclosureSheriff, after a court judgmentFiled as a suit (ORS 88.010). Sale and redemption follow the execution-sale rules (ORS 88.106).
Execution sale on a money judgmentSheriffPublic oral auction between 9 a.m. and 4 p.m. (ORS 18.930).

The rest of this page centers on the sheriff side, which is governed by chapters 18, 86 and 88 of the Oregon Revised Statutes.

How the sheriff gives notice of a real property sale

Notice goes out four ways at once: a website, a newspaper, the mail and the property itself. ORS 18.924 sets the steps for a sale of real property.

  • The sheriff posts the notice on the legal notices website for at least 28 days.
  • The notice also runs in a county newspaper once a week for four successive weeks.
  • At least 28 days before the sale, the sheriff mails it to the debtor by first-class and certified mail, and to the debtor's attorney and listed persons by first-class mail.
  • If a street address is given, a copy is posted on the property within seven days after the mailing.

The judgment creditor supplies the list of people who must be told. For real property, ORS 18.918 includes the debtor, any attorney named in the judgment, later lienholders and people who recorded interests from the debtor in a set window. In a foreclosure judgment, the list is the parties to the action. A missed name does not void the sale, but the creditor's certification can draw sanctions.

How the sale works, and postponements

It is a public oral auction held between 9 a.m. and 4 p.m. The judgment creditor must give the sheriff any title report at least 10 days before the first set sale date, and a county may collect a fee at the sale (ORS 18.930).

Several rules limit who buys and how much is sold. The sheriff sells only what is necessary to satisfy the judgment, and the sheriff and deputies cannot buy at the sale or take an interest because of it (ORS 18.934).

Postponements are built into the statute. Under ORS 18.932 the sheriff may postpone if the sale cannot proceed at the noticed time, if there are no buyers, or for other sufficient cause. The sheriff must postpone on the creditor's request, up to the return date. Multiple postponements are allowed, and no new notice of sale is needed.

Treat a date printed on a notice as a starting point, since a creditor's request or other cause can move it.

What happens right after the sale?

The sheriff prepares a certificate of sale, and the purchaser records it in the County Clerk Lien Record. ORS 18.942 requires the certificate to state whether the property is subject to redemption.

A real property sale is presumed to have been properly conducted unless the debtor or another affected person files an objection within 10 days after the sheriff's return is filed (ORS 18.948). If someone objects, the court holds a hearing and confirms the sale unless the objector shows the sale did not substantially conform to the law and probably caused damage. If the objection is sustained, the property is resold and the sheriff may not accept a bid below the first price.

The purchaser can take possession from the sale date until any redemption, and a tenant with an unexpired lease may stay through the redemption period by paying the greater of the value of use and occupancy or the lease payments (ORS 18.946). After a trustee's sale, the buyer is entitled to possession on the tenth day (ORS 86.782).

Redeeming a property after a sheriff sale

The people who can redeem are the judgment debtor, a mortgagor whose interest was sold, a junior lienholder, or a successor to any of them. ORS 18.963 lists them, and a person who has conveyed all of their interest to a successor cannot redeem.

The redemption windows are 180 days for the debtor and 60 days for a lien claimant (ORS 18.964). To redeem from the purchaser, the claimant pays the purchase price with interest at nine percent per year from the sale date. Taxes, costs to prevent waste, senior liens and homeowners' association assessments that the purchaser paid are added, each with nine percent interest from the date of payment (ORS 18.966).

Unless the debtor redeems, the sheriff delivers a deed to the certificate holder on request and payment of the statutory fee, as soon as possible (ORS 18.985). A court may order a deed early if the certificate holder has acquired all redemption rights.

What a homeowner can do before a foreclosure sale

A lender on a residential trust deed generally has to offer a resolution conference before it can foreclose. Under ORS 86.726, a lender that intends to foreclose a residential trust deed must first request a conference with the borrower, unless it qualifies for a limited exemption based on how few actions it filed the previous year.

Oregon Housing and Community Services runs the Foreclosure Avoidance Program. Here is how it works in practice:

  • The Department of Justice oversees the program, and a Mediation Case Manager handles day-to-day operations.
  • Homeowners pay a fee to the case manager, meet a housing counselor, submit documents, and attend the conference with a neutral facilitator.
  • Low-income homeowners may have all but $50 of the fee waived.
  • Housing counselors are free, and OHCS keeps a list of approved agencies.
  • The lender must send a representative with full authority to negotiate, but it does not have to modify the loan.

The statute caps the grantor's fee at $200 and the lender's at $600, with the conference scheduled within 10 days of a request and held within 75 days after notice (ORS 86.729). If the fee deadline is missed, the case manager cancels the conference and issues a certificate of compliance, after which the lender may go ahead.

Phone numbers: the Mediation Case Manager at 855-658-6733, and the Department of Justice Consumer Protection Hotline at 877-877-9392 for scam reports.

Junior lienholders and judicial foreclosure timing

Junior lienholders have to be named in the suit, or they keep some rights. Under ORS 88.030, a junior holder left out of the case who does not redeem within five years of the sheriff's sale is barred from later action on that interest.

Other points in chapter 88 matter for owners:

  • Paying the amount due and costs before judgment dismisses the suit. Paying after judgment but before sale ends the judgment's effect for the amount paid (ORS 88.100).
  • A foreclosure judgment is enforced by execution. If the sale falls short, a money award can be enforced like an ordinary judgment (ORS 88.060).
  • For certain purchase-money mortgages, including seller-financed ones and some residential mortgages of $50,000 or less, the judgment remedies for unpaid amounts end at the sale (ORS 88.103).
  • A mortgage lien ends 10 years after the later of maturity, the end of the debt term or an agreed extension, with exceptions (ORS 88.110 and 88.120).

In a trustee's sale, a subsequent lienholder who did not get required notice gets the rights of an omitted junior lienholder in a judicial foreclosure, and those are the exclusive remedies (ORS 86.767).

Extra time a trustee's sale adds

A trustee's sale adds a long runway and an extra publication step. Notice of sale must be served on an occupant at least 120 days before the sale, and it must run once a week for four successive weeks in a newspaper of general circulation, with the last publication more than 20 days before the sale (ORS 86.774).

The notice states the date, time and place of sale, and the right to reinstate no later than five days before the last date set (ORS 86.771). The sale may be postponed for periods totaling no more than 180 days from the original date, and notice of a new date must be given at least 15 days ahead unless the postponement is two calendar days or less (ORS 86.782).

The trustee delivers the deed within 10 days after the purchaser pays, and may rescind within 10 calendar days after the sale only on listed grounds, such as a bona fide error. A homeowner who wants to avoid the auction altogether has the most room to act during this long notice period, whether that means reinstating the loan or selling the house.

Frequently asked questions

How long do I have to redeem my house after an Oregon sheriff sale?

A judgment debtor has 180 days after the sale. A lien claimant has 60 days. The redemption price is the purchase price plus nine percent yearly interest and any taxes or senior liens the buyer paid (ORS 18.964 and 18.966).

Can an Oregon sheriff sale be postponed?

Yes. The sheriff can postpone if the sale cannot go forward, if there are no buyers, or for other sufficient cause, and must postpone at the creditor's request up to the return date. A postponement does not require a new notice of sale (ORS 18.932).

Where is an Oregon foreclosure sale held?

A trustee's sale must be held in a county where the property is located, between 9 a.m. and 4 p.m. A sheriff sale is a public oral auction, also held between 9 a.m. and 4 p.m. (ORS 86.782 and 18.930).

Can the sheriff buy the property at the sale?

No. The sheriff and deputies may not buy property at the sale or get any interest in it because of the sale (ORS 18.934).

Is there free help for Oregon homeowners facing foreclosure?

Yes. The state Foreclosure Avoidance Program connects homeowners with free housing counselors and a resolution conference with their lender. The Mediation Case Manager's number is 855-658-6733.

Who can legally sell a house after an Oregon owner dies?

Usually the court-appointed personal representative, not an heir or a person named in the will. Under ORS 114.215, title to a dead person's property passes to the heirs or devisees, but it stays subject to administration and sale by the personal representative. That representative takes possession and control of the estate under ORS 114.225.

The Oregon Real Estate Agency gives brokers the same warning. Being named in a will or being an heir does not by itself give someone the right to sell. Brokers are told to stop if probate has not been filed, the death was very recent, someone calls themselves executor without going through the court, there are several heirs, or no attorney is involved.

So before any buyer can close, someone has to hold court papers showing an appointment, or the estate has to qualify for a shortened procedure.

Getting appointed as personal representative

An interested person, or the person nominated in the will, files a petition with the circuit court. ORS 113.035 requires the petition to list the heirs and devisees and estimate the extent of the assets.

When more than one person wants the job, ORS 113.085 sets the order of preference:

  • The personal representative named in the will
  • The surviving spouse
  • Intestate heirs who receive a share
  • Other people who receive a share
  • The director of the state human services or health agency, or an approved attorney
  • The state's department for former service members, then anyone else

If a person dies with no will and no known heirs, the State Treasurer is appointed, and ORS 113.238 requires notice to the Treasurer within 48 hours of learning of such a death. The court sets any bond based on the estate's assets, income and debts (ORS 113.105). Marion County's court lays out the general path: petition, appointment, collecting assets, paying debts, an accounting to the court, and distribution.

Does the judge have to approve the sale?

In most estates, no. ORS 114.325 gives the representative power to sell, mortgage or lease estate property without notice, a hearing or a court order.

There are two exceptions. A sale needs notice, a hearing and an order if it would go against the terms of the will. The same is true if the house was specifically left to someone and the will does not authorize a sale. If the representative will not act, ORS 114.335 lets an interested person ask the court to order a sale.

A few rules protect the buyer:

  • A buyer who deals with the representative without actual knowledge of an improper act is protected as if the power were properly used (ORS 114.385).
  • The buyer does not have to track how the sale money is later spent.
  • Property sold by a representative stays subject to liens against the decedent or the estate, but not to creditor claims against the heirs (ORS 114.345).
  • A sale to the representative or to certain related parties is voidable unless an exception applies (ORS 114.355).

Probate timeline

Plan on several months at minimum. In Marion County, probate takes at least four months, most cases close in under a year, and the average runs six to nine months.

Most of that schedule comes from a handful of fixed clocks in the statutes.

Probate steps and their deadlines
StepDeadline
Information to heirs and devisees (ORS 113.145)Within 30 days of appointment
Search for creditors (ORS 115.003)3 months after appointment, unless the court allows longer
Notice to known claimants (ORS 115.003)Within 30 days after the search period ends
Claims barred if not presented (ORS 115.005)Later of 4 months after published notice or 45 days after a mailed notice
Will contest (ORS 113.075)4 months after the heirs information is delivered or mailed
Supplemental inventory for later-found property (ORS 113.175)Within 30 days of learning of it
Notice of final account and distribution (ORS 116.093)Mailed at least 20 days before the objection date

A sale can usually close before the estate is fully wrapped up, because the representative already holds the power to sell. The proceeds then sit with the estate until the court approves distribution.

Probate costs and the representative's fee

Expect a filing fee, the cost of publishing notice, bond if one is required, attorney fees, and the representative's fee. Accountants, appraisers, repairs and sale costs are common extras.

The representative's commission follows a sliding scale in ORS 116.173:

  • 7 percent of the first $1,000
  • 4 percent of the amount from $1,000 up to $10,000
  • 3 percent of the amount from $10,000 up to $50,000
  • 2 percent of anything above $50,000

The fee can be waived, and the court may allow extra pay for unusual work. The representative also needs court approval before paying representative or attorney fees or handing property to heirs.

The percentages apply to the property the court supervises, so a higher sale price raises the fee. Heirs choosing between a quick sale and a long listing should ask the estate attorney to run both numbers.

Creditors and unpaid bills

Creditors must present claims to the personal representative. Filing a claim with the court does not count. ORS 115.005 bars a claim that is not presented in time, and ORS 115.025 requires it in writing with the amount, if known, and the claimant's name and address.

When the estate cannot pay everyone, ORS 115.125 sets a ranking. Support obligations and costs of administration come first. Wages earned in the 90 days before death rank above general creditors, and all other claims land at the bottom, paid in proportion within their class.

Liens on the house itself are a separate matter. Under ORS 114.345 a sale by the representative does not wipe out liens that attached to the decedent's property. They are usually paid from the sale money at closing, which is one reason heirs ask for a payoff statement early.

What if no personal representative has been appointed and the house sits empty?

The family has two options: start probate, or check whether a shortened procedure fits the estate. Signing a purchase contract does not skip either one. Brokers are told to pause and send the person to an attorney when there are no court papers.

Once a representative is appointed, ORS 114.265 directs the representative to settle the estate as promptly as is reasonable and with as little loss of value as possible. For a vacant house, that is a good reason to decide early whether to repair and list it or sell it as is. A cash sale skips the repairs, showings and open houses, though the representative's authority still has to be in place before closing.

Local court differences

The statutes are the same statewide, but each circuit court posts its own forms, hours and local practice. A county court page typically offers forms, a fee schedule reference and a plain summary of what the representative must do. Marion County's also points to ways property can pass outside court, such as jointly owned accounts with survivorship and payable-on-death accounts.

Heirs who live out of state still need the same court appointment before a buyer can close. Calling the local court clerk for forms is a sensible first step.

Final account and distribution after the house sells

The representative files an account and asks the court to approve distribution. ORS 116.083 requires the account to cover the period, money and property received, payments made and property on hand, with a declaration under penalty of perjury.

The final account adds statements that required estate tax returns and Oregon taxes are filed or paid, a statement of the representative's pay, and a petition for a judgment of distribution. If all distributees consent in writing and every creditor is paid in full, a simpler statement can replace the full account.

The representative must keep estate money in a separate account in the representative's name, so closing proceeds go there. Bring the closing statement and the account details to the attorney so the sale shows up correctly in the final account.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Can I sell my parent's house in Oregon if I am the only child and there is no will?

Not on your own signature until you have authority. Being the only heir does not by itself let you sign a sale. The usual route is to petition for appointment as personal representative, and ORS 113.085 puts surviving heirs high in the order of preference after a spouse. A small estate may qualify for a shorter procedure, so ask an attorney which path fits.

Does the court have to approve the sale price of an inherited Oregon house?

Usually not. ORS 114.325 lets a personal representative sell without a hearing or court order. A court order is needed if the sale would go against the will, or if the house was specifically left to someone and the will gives no power to sell.

How long do creditors have to make claims against the estate?

Four months after the published notice, or 45 days after a mailed notice, whichever is later. The claim has to be presented to the personal representative, not just filed with the court (ORS 115.005).

Can a broker list a house right after the owner dies?

Only once legal authority is confirmed. If probate has not been filed, there are several heirs, or no attorney is involved, the Oregon Real Estate Agency advises brokers to pause and recommend counsel.

Who gets the money if the house sells during probate?

The estate does. The proceeds go into the estate account, and the court must approve fees and any distribution to heirs. What is left after debts, taxes and costs goes to the heirs or devisees under the will or Oregon intestacy law.
